strengths: Substantial system contribution: NeuroBuds is a well-motivated, low-cost (~$80, 20g, 8-channel) earphone-based ExG platform that enables free-living data collection, and DailySense is a genuinely novel dataset spanning tasks across five human senses.

PiMT is a sensible, well-motivated idea: physiology-informed fixed sub-band filter banks give the encoder explicit access to task-relevant spectral components, and the ablation (1/2/4/12 bands) plus saliency analysis (Figure 4) provide reasonable evidence that multi-band tokenization helps and that the model attends to physiologically plausible bands.

Broad evaluation: DailySense plus four public benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCI IV 2b), with comparisons to a range of baselines, LOSO and cross-session/cross-subject analyses, pre-training data-scale study, patch-size and pre-training-component ablations, and an on-device deployment analysis.
Good breadth of supporting material (hardware, signal quality, protocols, hyperparameters), and the paper is generally well written and clearly structured.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol likely inflates the headline results: the main results use an 80/20 random split over randomly shuffled, non-overlapping 4-second windows (Appendix F). Consecutive windows from the same session/subject are highly correlated, so this is effectively within-session evaluation prone to leakage. This is corroborated by the authors' own Table 7: cross-session drops to 0.700 F1 and cross-subject to 0.586 — far below the headline 0.876. The abstract and conclusion emphasize the within-session numbers without this caveat.

Cross-subject results undermine the central generalization claim: in Table 7, PiMT is actually worse than PatchTST on video/audio tasks and notably worse for gaze regression (7.78° vs 7.07°), yet the paper claims PiMT 'generalizes effectively to unseen users' (Section 5.6) and 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods'.

Missing comparisons with ExG foundation/self-supervised models that the paper itself positions against (BrainBERT, BIOT, BrainWave, LaBraM/whole-exg models); on public benchmarks only PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba are compared, and no previously published SOTA numbers are referenced, making 'state-of-the-art' claims hard to verify.

Internal inconsistencies that raise concerns about rigor: pre-training corpus stated as 50 hours in Section 5.1 but 'entire 40 hours' in Appendix G; Mamba backbone described as 8 layers/hidden 16 in Appendix F but 16 layers in Appendix G; EEG-beta given as 13–30 Hz in Section 3.1 but 12–30 Hz in Figure 8; EMG-HF stated as 95–100 Hz but '95–' in figures; Table 3 lists 'Scent paper' as the rough-texture material for the touch task (apparent error); taste and smell both use vinegar as the 'sour' stimulus, creating potential stimulus confounds.

Small and potentially confounded labeled data: task-specific data involves up to 7 participants per task with very short recordings (e.g., 300 seconds per class for taste/smell), so per-task F1 estimates have high variance; the dataset may not be released ('working with our legal team'), limiting reproducibility of the core contribution.

Baseline comparison is asymmetric: only PatchTST has a tailored pre-training strategy; all other baselines are evaluated without pre-training. The claimed 5.7% pre-training gain for PiMT vs 0.8% for PatchTST conflates the benefit of the multi-band tokenization architecture with the benefit of free-living pre-training data; a controlled decomposition (e.g., PiMT architecture without pre-training vs. PatchTST with the same pre-training) is only partially addressed.

The ablation results are within noise of the full model (Table 4: several 'w/o' variants exceed the full model on individual tasks, e.g., w/o P gives better gaze error 5.98° vs 6.00°), weakening claims that all six reconstruction objectives are needed; the six-task pre-training design appears largely heuristic without justification for the specific objective set.
Gaze tracking utility is questionable: ~6° mean angular error is coarse for interaction use, and the paper does not compare against any EOG-specific gaze-tracking baseline.

strengths: Ambitious end-to-end contribution spanning hardware (NeuroBuds earphone-based ExG prototype), dataset curation (DailySense, free-living + five-senses tasks), and a training method (PiMT), with IRB approval and detailed appendices (hardware, protocols, ablations, cross-session/cross-subject analysis, on-device deployment).

The multi-band tokenization idea is sensible and physiologically motivated, and the band-count ablation (Figure 3) plus saliency analysis (Figure 4) provide some evidence that fine-grained spectral decomposition helps and yields task-relevant band activations.
Honest reporting in the appendix: cross-subject (58.6%) and cross-session (70.0%) results and LOSO experiments are disclosed, and limitations including personalization challenges are acknowledged.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol has a serious data-leakage flaw. All headline results (Tables 1, 2) use a random 80/20 split over shuffled 4-second windows from the same continuous recordings/sessions. Contiguous, highly correlated windows appear in both train and test, inflating within-session performance (e.g., 0.964 F1 on Video). The appendix cross-subject result (0.586) shows the leaked numbers are not representative of real-world utility, yet the abstract, introduction, and conclusions emphasize the inflated within-session gains.

Missing comparison to actual state-of-the-art ExG methods. On public benchmarks (SEED, DREAMER, Sleep-EDF, BCI IV-2b) the paper only compares against PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba, while cited foundation-model baselines (BIOT, BrainBERT, BrainWave, Large Brain Model/UniTrans) are absent. 'Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art' is therefore unsupported.

Limited novelty. PiMT is a combination of well-known components: fixed band-pass filter banks (standard in EEG/EMG processing), patch tokenization (PatchTST), bidirectional Mamba, and MAE-style reconstruction. The 'physiology-informed' framing is a design heuristic, not a methodological advance.

Pre-training corpus is very small (50 hours, 22 subjects) for foundation-model claims, and the reported pre-training gain (0.819→0.876) may partially reflect subject overlap between pre-training and fine-tuning data rather than transferable representations; the main results do not isolate this.

Reproducibility concerns: the core DailySense dataset is not released ('working with our legal team'), and the benchmark's value as 'the first five-senses benchmark' cannot be verified. Prior work on taste/smell EEG exists (which the paper itself cites), weakening the 'first' claim.

Internal inconsistencies undermine rigor: Appendix F says 8 layers/hidden 16/embedding 64 while Appendix G says 16 layers/hidden dimension 16; pre-training data is stated as 50 hours in the main text but '40 hours' in Appendix G; Figure 1 caption uses 'PiFT'; Appendix B cites gaze accuracy 'as shown in Appendix I' where that content does not appear.

Dataset and tasks are small and weakly powered: up to ~7 participants per labeled task, binary labels (rough/smooth, sweet/sour, interesting/not), and only 20 hours of task data; EEG-based claims for smell/taste tasks are controversial and require more careful validation (e.g., controlling for muscle artifacts, swallowing, respiration).

Ablation results in Table 4 are nearly flat (full model 0.876 vs. ablations 0.871–0.874), suggesting the six pre-training objectives add little; several individual components even outperform the full model on specific tasks, and no statistical significance testing is reported anywhere.

Claim framing exceeds evidence: '87% average F1 over baseline models' conflates the leaked within-session setting, and the deployment analysis evaluates a Transformer surrogate rather than the actual Mamba model.

strengths: A substantial end-to-end systems contribution: NeuroBuds is a low-cost ($80), lightweight ear-EEG/EMG/EOG prototype, and DailySense is a novel free-living ExG dataset (50h unlabeled + 20h labeled) spanning five human senses, which is a genuinely useful resource for the community.

The physiology-informed multi-band tokenization idea is intuitive and well-motivated, and the ablation over 1/2/4/12 bands (Figure 3) plus saliency analysis (Figure 4) provides some evidence that fine-grained spectral decomposition helps and aligns with known physiology.

Broad evaluation surface: six DailySense tasks plus four public ExG benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCIC IV-2b), with multiple seeds, LOSO, cross-session/cross-subject analyses, backbone comparison, patch-size ablation, pre-training component ablation, and on-device deployment analysis.
Comprehensive appendices covering hardware design, signal quality, data collection protocols, and hyperparameters, which supports partial reproducibility of the method (if not the data).
weaknesses: Potentially serious evaluation flaw: the main results use a random 80/20 split over shuffled 4-second windows taken from continuous recordings, i.e., a within-session random split. Adjacent windows from the same continuous recording are highly correlated, so train/test leakage is likely; the very high within-session scores (0.96 F1 for video/audio) are plausibly inflated. The standard protocol for such tasks is cross-session or cross-subject evaluation, where the method's advantage largely disappears (Table 7: PiMT is worse than PatchTST on video/audio and gaze in the cross-subject setting).

The central claim that PiMT 'consistently outperforms' state-of-the-art methods is not fully supported: in cross-subject evaluation PiMT underperforms PatchTST on several tasks (e.g., 0.612 vs 0.654 on video, 7.78° vs 7.07° gaze error), and cross-session gains are modest. The abstract and introduction overstate the evidence.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: pre-training corpus is described as 50 hours in the main text but 40 hours in Appendix G; 70 hours total is claimed in the discussion; Mamba is described as 8 layers/hidden 16 in Appendix F but 16 layers/hidden 16 in Appendix G; memory usage is 3.1% in the main text vs 3.6% in Table 6; Sleep-EDF is described as having EEG sampled at 100 Hz but '1000 Hz' appears in the Discussion; Appendix G also cites standard protocol for public benchmarks while Appendix E says a random 80/20 split was used, which is not the standard protocol for these datasets and precludes comparison to published state-of-the-art numbers.

Comparisons on public benchmarks are only against PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba re-implementations rather than published results of ExG foundation models (e.g., BIOT, BrainWave, LaBraM/EEGPT-style models), making the 'state-of-the-art' claim difficult to verify.

Methodological novelty is limited: PiMT is essentially a fixed band-pass filter bank + patching + a learnable linear tokenizer + Bidirectional-Mamba + MAE-style reconstruction pre-training, each drawn from prior work; the pre-training ablation (Table 4) shows nearly all components contribute marginally (drops of ~0.001–0.005, some ablations even improve video F1), weakening the claim that the six reconstruction tasks are important.

Pre-training and fine-tuning participants substantially overlap on DailySense; while LOSO is provided, the headline within-session numbers benefit from subject/session overlap, and the dataset itself is small (22 participants, 50h) for a 'foundation model' framing.
Dataset release is uncertain ('working with our legal team to determine the possibility of sharing'), which weakens reproducibility of the main claims; no code release is mentioned.

Scalability analysis (Figure 5) shows only pre-training loss decreasing with data scale, which is trivially expected; the downstream gains saturate quickly, offering weak evidence for the 'scales effectively' narrative.

Saliency analysis is qualitative and could plausibly reflect EMG artifacts (e.g., chewing, facial movement) rather than genuine neural correlates of touch/taste/smell, but the paper does not control for this obvious confound—particularly problematic since many 'sensory' tasks likely co-occur with distinct motor behaviors.

strengths: Integrated co-design contribution: a low-cost earphone-based ExG hardware prototype (NeuroBuds), a new free-living dataset (DailySense) spanning five human senses, and a task-agnostic training framework (PiMT) — a substantial system-level contribution beyond a pure algorithmic paper.

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons against 8 baselines, four public benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCI IV 2b), tokenization ablations (raw/STFT/CWT), backbone ablation (Mamba vs. Transformer), pre-training component ablations, patch-size sensitivity, frozen-encoder evaluation, LOSO and cross-session/cross-subject settings, on-device runtime analysis, and paired Wilcoxon significance tests — unusually thorough for this area.
Honest reporting of limitations, including the significant cross-subject performance drop and the inter-subject variability challenge, which strengthens credibility.

The appendix comparison of pre-training on free-living DailySense data versus much larger controlled corpora (TUAR/TUSZ, up to 498.6 hrs) is a valuable finding supporting the free-living data hypothesis.

Saliency analysis provides physiological interpretation, showing task-relevant band activation without supervision, and hardware validation against OpenBCI (correlation ~0.71–0.76) supports signal quality claims.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of the core method: PiMT is essentially fixed band-pass filter banks + patch tokenization + reconstruction pre-training on a Mamba backbone; each ingredient is well-established, and the assembly, while sensible, is incremental relative to existing EEG foundation-model work (BIOT, BrainBERT, LaBraM, etc.).

Main DailySense evaluation uses within-session random 80/20 splits of adjacent 4-second windows, which is prone to temporal autocorrelation leakage and inflates absolute performance; the honest cross-session (0.70) and cross-subject (0.586) results in the appendix are much lower, and the cross-subject gain over PatchTST (0.580) is within noise, weakening the generalization claims in the abstract.

Validity concern for the 'five senses' tasks: the saliency analysis itself notes that touch/taste/smell/audio activations align with peri-auricular EMG from near-ear muscle movements, suggesting the model may be classifying movement/behavioral confounds rather than genuinely decoding sensory processing; no artifact-control experiments (e.g., conditioned on chewing/EMG-only baselines) are provided to rule this out.

Modest scale and confounded comparison for a 'foundation model' framing: 50 hours / 22 participants is small, task data has as few as ~6-7 participants per task, and DailySense is self-collected and (still) not released ('working with our legal team'), limiting reproducibility of the headline benchmark; the claim that free-living data beats larger controlled corpora could partially reflect domain match between pre-training and the DailySense test distribution rather than intrinsic data superiority.

Inconsistencies and unclear details: the cross-system correlation is reported as 0.71 in text but 0.7586 in the figure caption; ECG bands (0.03–0.488 Hz) seem implausible for an ear-worn device and their role is unexplained; PiMT vs. Bidirectional-Mamba raw-signal baseline in Table 8 appears identical in places, raising questions about whether the tokenization or the backbone drives gains.
On-device deployment results use a Transformer substitute rather than the actual Mamba model, so the reported 25 ms latency does not reflect the real system.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically meaningful problem—task-agnostic ExG representation learning from unobtrusive wearable hardware—and presents a genuine system co-design (NeuroBuds hardware, DailySense dataset, PiMT training) rather than a purely algorithmic contribution.

Experimental coverage is broad: six tasks on the new dataset, four public benchmarks (DREAMER, SEED, Sleep-EDF, BCI IV-2b), ablations over tokenization strategies, patch sizes, pre-training components, backbone choices, data scale, frozen-encoder evaluation, LOSO, cross-session/cross-subject splits, statistical significance tests, and on-device deployment measurements.

The hardware validation against a research-grade OpenBCI device (correlation ~0.71) and the comparison of free-living vs. controlled pre-training corpora (TUAR/TUSZ) are useful, transparent additions.
The saliency analysis relating frequency-band tokens to task physiology provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for why multi-band tokenization helps.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. PiMT is essentially fixed hand-crafted filter-bank decomposition + patch embedding + Bidirectional-Mamba + masked/autoencoding reconstruction—a combination of existing, well-known components (PatchTST-style patching, BrainBERT/BIOT-style reconstruction pre-training, Vision-Mamba backbone). The 'physiology-informed' bands are largely textbook band definitions, several of which heavily overlap (e.g., EEG-beta 13–30 Hz vs. EMG-LF 15–45 Hz, EEG-gamma 30–100 Hz vs. EMG-MF 45–95 Hz), so the '12 distinct physiological modalities' framing is overstated.

Evaluation protocol raises leakage concerns on the headline results. The main DailySense results use a random 80/20 window-level split within each participant after segmenting contiguous recordings into 4-second windows; adjacent windows are highly correlated, so the impressive 0.96 F1 numbers likely reflect temporal near-duplication between train and test. The more realistic cross-session (0.700) and cross-subject (0.586) results show much weaker performance, and in the cross-subject setting PiMT actually underperforms PatchTST on several tasks (video, audio) and on gaze (7.78° vs. 7.07°), contradicting the claim that PiMT 'consistently outperforms' baselines.

Unfair or incomplete baseline comparisons. Only PatchTST receives a pre-training counterpart; other strong ExG self-supervised/foundation baselines (BIOT, LaBraM, BrainWave, EEG foundation models) are absent from the main tables. On public benchmarks PiMT is compared against only two baselines, and the reported SEED result (0.820) is far below what even the authors' own standardized protocol yields (0.971 in Table 5), which is confusing and undermines confidence in the benchmark evaluation.

Attribution of gains is muddied. Table 8 shows raw-signal tokenization with the same backbone achieves 0.779 average F1 vs. PiMT's 0.819 without pre-training, and Table 6 shows pre-training alone gives Bidirectional-Mamba 0.813. The composite improvement over the strongest baseline is thus modest, while the paper attributes gains jointly to PiMT + pre-training + hardware data without cleanly disentangling them (Appendix I helps but is not fully convincing).

Scale and dataset concerns. 50 hours of free-living data and 6–9 participants per labeled task is very small for 'foundation model' claims; several tasks (taste, smell) are binary with self-reported labels and few subjects, and the touch/smell results may reflect peri-auricular EMG confounds (movement during stimulation) rather than perception itself, which the paper itself half-acknowledges in the saliency discussion.

Reproducibility is weak: the DailySense dataset is not released ('working with our legal team'), the hardware prototype is not available, and the strongest results depend on a proprietary dataset. Ablation results (Table 7) show some individual components outperform the full model (e.g., w/o P gives 5.98° vs. 6.00° gaze), and gains over ablations are within noise ranges, further weakening the 'complementary benefit' claim.

Positioning and writing issues: the claim that Bidirectional-Mamba 'has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance' cites unrelated works (Zerveas 2021, Song 2022); the abstract's 'average F1-score of 87.6% over baseline models' is confusingly phrased (it is an absolute average F1, not an improvement); and the five-senses framing is more marketing than scientific necessity.

strengths: Integrated systems contribution: the NeuroBuds earphone prototype ($80, 20g, 8-channel ADS1299/ESP32 design), validated against a research-grade OpenBCI device (Pearson r = 0.71/0.7586), addresses a genuine gap in scalable, free-living ExG data collection.

DailySense is a genuinely novel benchmark: the first ear-ExG dataset spanning all five human senses with 50 hours of free-living data plus 20 hours of labeled task data, with a detailed protocol (Table 3) and IRB approval.

PiMT is a sensible, well-motivated task-agnostic design: physiology-informed multi-band decomposition plus patch tokenization and a Bidirectional-Mamba encoder removes task-specific band filtering, and the ablation showing monotonic gains from 1-, 2-, 4-, to 12-band tokenization (Figure 3) directly supports the core claim.

Unusually thorough evaluation for this area: paired Wilcoxon significance tests (Appendix P), LOSO evaluation, cross-subject/cross-session splits, frozen-encoder evaluation, patch-size sensitivity, STFT/CWT tokenization comparisons, pre-training data-scale analysis, comparison against larger controlled pre-training corpora (TUAR/TUSZ, Appendix Q), and on-device deployment (25 ms latency, ONNX).
Honest discussion of limitations (Section 6), including inter-subject variability and modest dataset scale.
The paper cleanly separates contributions: ablations (Table 6, Appendix I) show both the pre-training and the tokenization components independently add value.
weaknesses: The headline within-session results (e.g., F1 0.964 for video, 0.876 average) appear inflated by likely data leakage: random 80/20 splits over shuffled 4-second windows from continuous recordings mean adjacent, highly correlated windows span train and test sets. This concern is substantiated by the paper's own cross-subject results (Table 12), where PiMT drops to near-chance 0.586 average F1, suggesting the within-session numbers overstate practical utility and that the framing of 'state-of-the-art' rests on a weak evaluation protocol.

The 'task-agnostic foundation model' narrative is undercut by the near-chance cross-subject performance (0.586 vs. 0.580 for PatchTST; gaze error actually worsens from 6.42° to 7.78° vs. PatchTST in the cross-subject setting). The claimed generalization largely holds only within-session/cross-session.

PiMT's technical novelty is moderate: it is a combination of existing components (fixed filter banks grounded in textbook physiology, PatchTST-style patching, Bidirectional-Mamba, masked reconstruction à la MAE/BrainBERT/BIOT). Overlapping, hand-picked bands (e.g., EEG-gamma 30–100 Hz overlapping EMG-LF 15–45 Hz; ECG-HF 0.12–0.488 Hz applied to ear channels) raise questions about how 'physiology-informed' versus heuristic the tokenization really is; no learned- or random-band comparison is provided beyond the coarse 1/2/4/12-band sweep.

Public benchmark comparisons omit recent ExG-specific self-supervised foundation models (e.g., BIOT, LaBraM, BENDR, LaBraM-class models), even though such methods are directly cited; comparing only against PatchTST and Bidirectional-Mamba weakens the SOTA claim on DREAMER/SEED/Sleep-EDF/BCI IV 2b.

Labeled data is small and binary: 6–9 participants per task, binary classification for taste/touch/smell/interest, with subjects up to 62 years old but limited demographic diversity; some downstream tasks (e.g., 'interest inference') have ambiguous construct validity relative to the ground-truth labels.
Reproducibility of the central resource is uncertain: the dataset release is still 'being determined with the legal team,' so the main artifact may not be available; no code release is stated.

Some result inconsistencies and loose claims: gaze improvements are small (~0.4°) relative to reported standard deviations; STFT's 9.04° gaze error in Table 8 is surprising and under-analyzed; the salary of an 8.5% Mamba-vs-Transformer gain (Appendix H) conflates backbone choice with the paper's core contribution.
The Wilcoxon procedure pools participant–seed combinations as independent paired samples (Appendix P), which treats non-independent seeds as independent observations and may overstate significance.
